---
title: "Getting started with tidy data"
---

Explore Education Statistics (EES) is the service DfE uses to publish official
statistics. This guide is for people new to preparing tidy data for EES. You
don't need any experience with tidy data to follow it.

It explains what tidy data is, then works through an example from a table to
a finished data file and metadata file, with optional R and Python scripts.
It ends with checklists to use before publication.

Tidy data is the foundation of a statistics release in EES. From the same
tidy data files, you can:

- create tables and charts for your release
- let users build their own tables, selecting the information they need
- make data available to download or reuse through the API

The [Open Data Standards](ud.qmd) provide the full technical reference,
including exceptions and accepted values. If you plan to publish through
the API, you should also follow the
[API data standards](api-data-standards.qmd).

## What is tidy data?

Tidy data is a way of organising information so that:

1. **Each column represents one variable** — something you are measuring
   or describing, such as a year, region or number of pupils.
2. **Each row represents one observation** — one particular combination
   of those variables.
3. **Each cell contains one value.**

These principles make data easier to analyse, combine, filter and reuse.

### An example: pupil numbers by year and sex

Imagine you have a table showing the number of pupils in two regions,
broken down by year and sex.

| Region | 2024_male | 2024_female | 2025_male | 2025_female |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| North East | 24,300 | 22,700 | 24,500 | 22,900 |
| North West | 67,200 | 63,100 | 67,600 | 63,500 |

*Illustrative figures for explaining tidy data.*

This is a useful table for someone to read. But there are two pieces of
information hidden inside every numerical column heading: **year** and
**sex**.

The same information in a tidy structure looks like this:

| region_name | year | sex | pupil_count |
|---|---|---|---:|
| North East | 2024 | Male | 24,300 |
| North East | 2024 | Female | 22,700 |
| North East | 2025 | Male | 24,500 |
| North East | 2025 | Female | 22,900 |
| North West | 2024 | Male | 67,200 |
| North West | 2024 | Female | 63,100 |
| North West | 2025 | Male | 67,600 |
| North West | 2025 | Female | 63,500 |

The figures haven't changed. We've just organised them differently.

Instead of having separate columns for every combination of year and sex,
we now have:

- a `region_name` column identifying the region
- a `year` column identifying the year
- a `sex` column identifying the pupils' sex
- a `pupil_count` column containing the number of pupils

Each row represents one observation. For example, the first row tells us
that there were 24,300 male pupils in the North East in 2024.

### Why is this better?

The tidy table is longer, but the structure stays the same when new
information is added.

For example, if we wanted to include 2026, we would **add more rows,
rather than more columns**.

We could also filter the data to just female pupils, compare years, or
combine it with other data using the same variables.

This is particularly useful for software. Rather than writing code that
handles a different column for every year and sex, we can use the same
columns each time.

**The key principle is to put categories into columns of their own,
rather than hiding them in column headings.**

## Worked example {#worked-example}

Let's work through a more realistic example of preparing pupil statistics
for EES.

We'll start with an Excel-style table containing pupil counts by academic
year, region, sex and education phase.

You can download the
[source CSV](../resources/open-data-standards/pupil-source.csv) and follow
the example using the figures for the North East in 2022/23.

There are three stages:

1. [Rearrange the existing counts](#rearrange-existing-counts).
2. [Add totals and percentages](#add-totals-and-percentages).
3. [Add EES time and geography fields](#add-ees-fields).

### 1. Rearrange the existing counts {#rearrange-existing-counts}

The source file has one row for each academic year and region, with
four numerical columns:

- `male_prim`: male primary pupils
- `female_prim`: female primary pupils
- `male_sec`: male secondary pupils
- `female_sec`: female secondary pupils

Here is the North East row for 2022/23, with descriptive headings
in place of the source's abbreviations.

```{r}
#| echo: false
read_example <- function(file) {
  read.csv(
    file.path("../resources/open-data-standards", file),
    colClasses = "character",
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}
show_table <- function(
  data, caption, col.names = names(data), big.mark = ",", ...
) {
  knitr::kable(
    data,
    row.names = FALSE,
    col.names = col.names,
    format.args = list(big.mark = big.mark),
    caption = caption,
    ...
  )
}

source_data <- read_example("pupil-source.csv")
example_data <- read_example("pupil-enrolments.csv")
example_meta <- read_example("pupil-enrolments.meta.csv")

source_counts <- c("male_prim", "female_prim", "male_sec", "female_sec")
source_data[source_counts] <- lapply(source_data[source_counts], as.integer)
example_data$pupil_count <- as.integer(example_data$pupil_count)
example_data$pupil_percent <- as.numeric(example_data$pupil_percent)

# North East rows for 2022/23, in the order they are shown on this page
north_east <- example_data[
  example_data$time_period == "202223" &
    example_data$region_code == "E12000001",
]
north_east <- north_east[order(
  match(
    north_east$education_phase,
    c("Primary", "Secondary", "All education phases")
  ),
  match(north_east$sex, c("Male", "Female", "Total"))
), ]

# The four counts that come straight from the source, without totals
north_east_detail <- north_east[
  north_east$education_phase != "All education phases" &
    north_east$sex != "Total",
]
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
show_table(
  source_data[
    source_data$academic_year == "2022/23" &
      source_data$region_name == "North East",
    c("region_name", source_counts)
  ],
  col.names = c(
    "Region", "Male primary", "Female primary",
    "Male secondary", "Female secondary"
  ),
  caption = "North East, 2022/23: the starting row (year column omitted)."
)
```

We can recognise the same problem as in the earlier example.
The numerical headings contain two pieces of information: the pupils'
sex and their education phase.

We want to make both of these into columns.

Here are the same four counts, rearranged into tidy data.

```{r}
#| echo: false
show_table(
  north_east_detail[
    , c("region_name", "sex", "education_phase", "pupil_count")
  ],
  col.names = c("Region", "Sex", "Phase", "Pupil count"),
  caption = paste(
    "North East, 2022/23: the same counts rearranged",
    "(year column omitted)."
  )
)
```

Nothing has been calculated or changed yet. We have simply moved
information out of the headings and into columns. This is often called
*pivoting* or *unpivoting*, depending on the software you're using.

The region repeats because each row needs to identify which pupils
the number describes.

Read the first row as: "In the North East, there are 13,100 male primary
pupils." Each row describes one combination of region, sex and education
phase for that year.

The year is still 2022/23 for each row. We'll add the standard EES
time columns in stage 3.

#### Understanding filters and indicators

EES uses two terms to describe the different types of columns in tidy data.

**Filters** are the categories that users can choose when exploring the data.

In our example, `sex` and `education_phase` are filters. A user can
choose male pupils, female pupils, primary pupils, secondary pupils
or combinations of these.

Keeping sex and phase in separate columns means users can select them
independently. A single category called "Female primary" would not give
users the same flexibility in the EES table tool.

**Indicators** are the things we measure.

All four numerical columns in our original table contain pupil counts.
They measure the same thing, so they belong in one indicator column:
`pupil_count`.

A useful question to ask when preparing your own data is:

- Does this column describe **which group** the figure relates to?
  It is probably a filter.
- Does it contain **the figure being measured**?
  It is probably an indicator.

We'll use these terms again when creating the metadata file.

### 2. Add totals and percentages {#add-totals-and-percentages}

Now that the counts are tidy, we need to decide what other figures
users will need.

The original source doesn't contain totals, so in this example we calculate:

- male and female pupils combined, using `Total` in the `sex` column
- primary and secondary pupils combined, using `All education phases`
  in the `education_phase` column
- the nine English regions combined, creating national rows for England

We also calculate the percentage of pupils of each sex within each
year, location and education phase.

For example, in the North East in 2022/23 there were 13,100 male and
11,900 female primary pupils, giving a total of 25,000.

The percentage of male primary pupils is calculated as:

**13,100 / 25,000 × 100 = 52.4%**

We have introduced another indicator, `pupil_percent`, alongside
`pupil_count`.

Because the counts and percentages describe the same groups of pupils,
they belong in the same tidy data file as separate columns.

Here are the complete North East figures for 2022/23, including
the totals and percentages.

```{r}
#| echo: false
north_east_rounded <- north_east[
  , c("education_phase", "sex", "pupil_count", "pupil_percent")
]
north_east_rounded$pupil_percent <- sprintf(
  "%.1f", north_east_rounded$pupil_percent
)
show_table(
  north_east_rounded,
  col.names = c("Phase", "Sex", "Pupil count", "Pupil percentage"),
  caption = paste(
    "North East, 2022/23: counts and percentages including totals,",
    "with percentages shown to 1 decimal place",
    "(time and geography columns omitted)."
  ),
  align = "llrr"
)
```

There are three choices for sex (`Male`, `Female`, `Total`) and three for
phase (`Primary`, `Secondary`, `All education phases`), giving nine rows for
the North East in 2022/23.

#### Be careful when adding totals

Totals are useful, but it's important not to count the same pupils
more than once.

For example, we can calculate:

13,100 male pupils + 11,900 female pupils = 25,000 pupils.

But adding the `Total` row to the male and female rows would give
50,000. That would count every pupil twice.

Similarly, we should only combine geographic areas or groups that
don't overlap, and we should not add percentages together to produce
a total.

When using the data, filters help users select the relevant groups
without including their totals as well.

You should also explain what each percentage is a percentage **of**
in your publication's public data guidance.

### 3. Add EES time and geography fields {#add-ees-fields}

We now have tidy data with the counts, totals and percentages we
want to publish.

Before uploading it to EES, we need to make sure each row contains
time and geography information in the standard format.

#### Time

In the source file, the year is recorded as `2022/23` in a column
called `academic_year`.

EES requires two columns to describe time:

| Column | Value |
|---|---|
| `time_period` | `202223` |
| `time_identifier` | `Academic year` |

These tell EES both the time period and the type of period being used.

Other formats, including calendar years and financial years, are
described in the [time columns guidance](ud.qmd#time-columns).

#### Geography

Each row also needs information about the geographic area it describes.

For the North East example, we need:

- `geographic_level`, identifying the type of geography
- `country_code` and `country_name`, identifying England
- `region_code` and `region_name`, identifying the North East

The North East region code is `E12000001`.

Here are all the standard time and geography values for the North East
rows in 2022/23.

```{r}
#| echo: false
location_columns <- c(
  "time_period", "time_identifier", "geographic_level",
  "country_code", "country_name", "region_code", "region_name"
)
show_table(
  data.frame(
    column = location_columns,
    value = unlist(north_east[1, location_columns], use.names = FALSE)
  ),
  col.names = c("Column in the data file", "Value on each row"),
  caption = "Time and geography fields for North East pupils in 2022/23."
)
```

Use geographic code lookups rather than entering codes manually.

If you work in R, the
[dfeR package](https://dfe-analytical-services.github.io/dfeR/) includes
geographic lookups such as
[`fetch_regions()`](https://dfe-analytical-services.github.io/dfeR/reference/fetch_regions.html).

You can also download the
[region lookup CSV](../resources/open-data-standards/pupil-region-lookup.csv)
used in this example.

#### Putting it all together

One row in our finished file describes:

- **When:** academic year 2022/23
- **Where:** North East
- **Who:** male primary pupils
- **How many:** 13,100 pupils
- **What percentage:** 52.4% of primary pupils in that region and year

All of this information is recorded in columns, so the row can be
understood independently of the other rows.

Here are some of the columns together, as they appear in the completed
data file.

```{r}
#| echo: false
show_table(
  north_east_detail[
    , c(
      "time_period", "time_identifier", "geographic_level",
      "region_name", "education_phase", "sex",
      "pupil_count", "pupil_percent"
    )
  ],
  caption = "Selected columns from the finished data file.",
  big.mark = ""
)
```

The [finished example data file](../resources/open-data-standards/pupil-enrolments.csv)
shows all the columns together.

The original source has 18 rows: two academic years for each of
the nine English regions. After rearranging the counts and adding totals,
percentages and England-level figures, the finished file has **180 rows**:

2 years × 10 locations × 3 phase categories × 3 sex categories.

The file is longer, but it gives people far more ways to explore the
same statistics.

## Try the example code

You can download working R and Python examples that turn the
original pupil table into the completed data file and its
[metadata file](#create-the-metadata), which is explained later in this guide.

These are optional. You don't need to run the scripts to understand
the steps in this guide.

**R example** (needs the dplyr, tidyr and dfeR packages)

- [prepare-pupil-example.R](../resources/open-data-standards/prepare-pupil-example.R)
- [pupil-source.csv](../resources/open-data-standards/pupil-source.csv)

**Python example** (needs the pandas package)

- [prepare-pupil-example.py](../resources/open-data-standards/prepare-pupil-example.py)
- [pupil-source.csv](../resources/open-data-standards/pupil-source.csv)
- [pupil-region-lookup.csv](../resources/open-data-standards/pupil-region-lookup.csv)

You can compare the files produced by the scripts against the:

- [finished data file](../resources/open-data-standards/pupil-enrolments.csv)
- [finished metadata file](../resources/open-data-standards/pupil-enrolments.meta.csv)

The values will match. The formatting can differ slightly between R and
Python, for example whether text is wrapped in quotation marks.

The scripts demonstrate the process for this particular example.
Your own data may have different categories, populations, missing
values or disclosure requirements that need additional handling.

**Make your data preparation repeatable.** Whether you work in
R, Python, SQL or SAS, it's good practice to prepare data using a
reproducible process that you can run again when new figures become
available.

See the [RAP guidance on preparing data](../RAP/rap-statistics/rap-statistics-preparing-data.qmd)
for further advice.

## Start from what you already have {#start-from-what-you-already-have}

Most teams already produce tables for their publications, perhaps
in Excel, from a database or using R, Python or SAS.

You don't necessarily need to create a tidy data file for every
existing table.

Instead, start by looking at the data behind those tables.

### Decide which figures belong together

In EES, users can create their own tables from the data you publish. The
table tool works with one data file at a time, so figures that people will
want to compare need to be in the same file.

Tables that describe the same underlying population can often be
combined into one tidy data file.

For example, you might currently publish separate tables for:

- pupil numbers by sex
- pupil numbers by education phase
- pupil numbers by sex and education phase

These can usually become one tidy data file, with filters for
sex and phase.

On the other hand, tables about substantially different subjects
or populations, such as pupil numbers and school finances, will
often make more sense as separate files.

Aim for a small number of useful files, without combining incompatible
data simply to reduce the count. Fewer files are more flexible for users
and give your team less to maintain and quality assure.

The [dataset design decisions](ud.qmd#dataset-design-decisions)
guidance explains these choices in more detail.

## Prepare the data file {#prepare-the-data-file}

Once you've decided which data belongs together and arranged it into
a tidy structure, you can prepare the CSV for EES.

### Use the required time and geography columns

As in [stage 3 of the worked example](#add-ees-fields), every data file
must contain the
[mandatory time and geography columns](ud.qmd#time-and-geography):
`time_period`, `time_identifier`, `geographic_level`, `country_code`
and `country_name`.

You also need the
[columns for each geographic level](ud.qmd#allowable-geographic-levels)
in your data. Our pupil example uses `region_code` and `region_name`.
These are left empty for the national rows, because those figures
describe England as a whole.

### Use consistent names and categories

Where standard categories exist, use the
[harmonised variables](ud.qmd#common-harmonised-variables).

For example, DfE uses `sex` with values such as `Male`, `Female`
and `Total`.

Using consistent names makes it easier to work with statistics
from different publications.

For other variables, follow the
[variable naming](ud.qmd#variable-names) and
[indicator naming](ud.qmd#indicator-names) guidance.

### Save the data in the correct format

Use a short, descriptive file name, such as `pupil-enrolments.csv`.

File names should be lower case, without spaces or years, so the
same name can be reused each release.

Save the data as a
[UTF-8 CSV](ud.qmd#how-to-export-data-with-utf-8-encoding), with:

- one row of column headings
- no separate title rows or row numbers
- geography codes stored as text
- percentages recorded as numbers, such as `52.4`, rather than
  `52.4%` or `0.524`

### Handle missing and suppressed values

Real datasets often contain missing, unavailable or confidential values.

EES has [standard data symbols](ud.qmd#data-symbols), including:

- `c` for confidential values
- `x` for unavailable values
- `z` for values that are not applicable

Don't use zero to represent these situations. Zero means the actual
value is zero.

Everything in your data file can be downloaded, so make sure your
disclosure control has been applied to the data itself before publishing.

## Create the metadata {#create-the-metadata}

Each tidy data file also needs a **metadata file**.

The data file contains the actual statistics. The metadata file
tells EES what the different columns mean and how to display them.

For example, our data file includes a column named `pupil_count`.
The metadata is where we tell EES to display this as **Number of pupils**,
with no decimal places.

### Start from the template

Download the
[blank metadata template](../resources/open-data-standards/metadata-template.meta.csv).

It contains the eight
[mandatory metadata columns](ud.qmd#mandatory-ees-metadata-columns).

You need one metadata row for each filter and indicator in your
data file. You do not need metadata rows for the standard time
and geography columns.

For our example, we need four rows: two filters and two indicators.
Each row gives the column's type and display label. Indicator rows also
set how the figure displays, such as its unit and number of decimal places.

Here are the main settings from the completed example.

```{r}
#| echo: false
show_table(
  example_meta[
    , c(
      "col_name", "col_type", "label", "indicator_unit",
      "indicator_dp", "filter_default"
    )
  ],
  caption = "Selected metadata settings for the pupil example."
)
```

In our example:

- `pupil_count` has no unit and displays with 0 decimal places
- `pupil_percent` uses `%` and displays with 1 decimal place
- filter rows leave indicator-specific metadata columns empty
- indicator rows leave filter-specific metadata columns empty

The name in `col_name` must exactly match the relevant column
heading in your data file.

### Set sensible default filters

You can also choose which filter values EES selects by default.

For this example, it makes sense to start with:

- `All education phases` for the phase filter
- `Total` for the sex filter

This gives users an overall pupil count when they first open
the data, while allowing them to select individual groups.

To do this, add the optional `filter_default` column to your metadata file.
It isn't in the template, so the completed example has nine columns
rather than eight.

The [aggregates and default filters guidance](ud.qmd#aggregates-and-default-filters)
explains how these settings work.

You can download the
[completed example metadata file](../resources/open-data-standards/pupil-enrolments.meta.csv)
to see the settings used.

### Name the metadata file

The metadata CSV must use the same base name as the data CSV,
with `.meta` added.

For example:

- Data: `pupil-enrolments.csv`
- Metadata: `pupil-enrolments.meta.csv`

These are the two files you'll upload to EES.

## Check your files {#check-your-files}

Before publishing, make sure both files meet the EES data standards.

EES automatically screens your data and metadata files when you
upload them, but you can run the same checks earlier using:

- the [EES data screener app](https://rsconnect/rsc/dfe-published-data-qa/),
  available on DfE kit
- the [eesyscreener R package](https://github.com/dfe-analytical-services/eesyscreener),
  which can be included in your data preparation pipeline

Fix any problems in your source data or code and regenerate the files,
rather than manually editing the final CSV.

Review warnings as well as errors. Passing the screening checks does
not replace your own quality assurance of the statistics, which is
covered in the [checklists](#checklists) below.

## Check how it looks in EES {#check-how-it-looks-in-ees}

Once you've [uploaded the files](ees.qmd#uploading-files), preview
your release in EES.

It's worth checking the data from the perspective of someone who
will use it, not just the perspective of the person who prepared it.

For our pupil example, try to:

1. Build a table comparing male and female primary pupils across regions.
2. Make a chart showing the percentage of pupils by sex.
3. Check that the indicator labels, units and decimal places are understandable.
4. Check that the default filter selections show sensible figures.
5. Create featured tables for the views users are most likely to need.

If you're replacing data in an existing publication, read the
[replacing data guidance](ees.qmd#replacing-data) before changing
column names or structures. These changes can affect tables and
charts that have already been set up.

If you are publishing through the API, also follow the
[API publishing checklist](api-data-standards.qmd#api-publishing-checklist).

## Checklists {#checklists}

### For each data file and metadata file

- [ ] Each row is an observation and the data has a
      [tidy structure](ud.qmd#tidy-data-structure).
- [ ] Filters and indicators are clearly identified.
- [ ] The [mandatory time and geography columns](ud.qmd#time-and-geography)
      are present.
- [ ] Column names follow the [naming standards](ud.qmd#variable-names),
      using [harmonised variables](ud.qmd#common-harmonised-variables)
      where appropriate.
- [ ] Missing and suppressed values use the
      [standard symbols](ud.qmd#data-symbols).
- [ ] The metadata file has
      [all mandatory columns](ud.qmd#mandatory-ees-metadata-columns),
      matching names and understandable labels.
- [ ] Both files are [UTF-8 CSVs](ud.qmd#data-format) with matching file names.
- [ ] The figures, totals and percentages have been checked against their
      sources.
- [ ] No combination of time, geography and filters appears more than once.
- [ ] Both files pass the
      [screening checks](ud.qmd#how-to-check-against-these-standards).

### For the whole publication

- [ ] Related data has been organised into a manageable number of useful files.
- [ ] Featured tables are available for the views users need most often.
- [ ] All published data meets the disclosure control policy.
- [ ] [Public data guidance](ees.qmd#public-data-guidance) and methodology
      explain what each file contains.
- [ ] Tables, charts and filter defaults have been checked in the EES preview.
- [ ] If publishing through the API, the
      [API publishing checklist](api-data-standards.qmd#api-publishing-checklist)
      is complete.

## Getting help

To upload and publish data, you need access to the EES admin system.
See [accessing EES](ees.qmd#accessing-ees).

For questions about tidy data, data standards or publishing in EES,
contact the Explore Education Statistics platforms team at
[explore.statistics@education.gov.uk](mailto:explore.statistics@education.gov.uk).
